Methotrexate is implicated in the pathogenesis of Acute Lymphoblastic/lymphocytic Leukemia (ALL) through a series of interconnected pathways, primarily involving the suppression of tumor cell proliferation and the modulation of immune responses. The evidence suggests that Methotrexate may act as a therapeutic agent for ALL through mechanisms that involve the inhibition of DNA synthesis and cell cycle progression, as indicated by its association with B-cell neoplasms and non-Hodgkin lymphoma. These conditions, in turn, are linked to ALL, suggesting a potential role for Methotrexate in the treatment of this leukemia subtype.

The integration of evidence from multiple paths highlights a shared mechanism of action involving the targeting of proliferative cells and the modulation of immune pathways, particularly through the involvement of Rituximab. While the direct link between Methotrexate and ALL remains indirect, the cumulative evidence points to a plausible mechanistic pathway that involves the suppression of tumor growth and the regulation of immune responses, which are critical in the pathogenesis of ALL. The presence of overlapping indications and the consistent association with Rituximab suggest that Methotrexate may exert its effects through a mechanism that is relevant to the treatment of ALL, though the exact nature of this mechanism remains to be fully elucidated.
